opus-5.5.text:
I think the distinction matters because they answer two fundamentally different questions, and people tend to conflate them.

Verification asks: does this program do what the specification says? That's a mathematical question. Once you have a formal spec, checking that the code satisfies it can, in principle, be done mechanically, with a proof checker or a theorem prover. Either the proof goes through or it doesn't. There's no judgment involved, and that's exactly what makes it so powerful when the code is written by an AI. You don't have to trust the model. You only have to trust a small, well-understood checker.

Validation asks something else: is the specification what we actually wanted? That can't be fully formalized, because it connects the formal world to human intent. Someone has to look at the spec and say, yes, this captures what I meant.

The reason I like separating them is that it shrinks the part that needs human attention. Today, if an AI writes ten thousand lines of code, a human has to review all ten thousand lines, and humans are bad at that. Bugs slip through. If you split the problem, the AI can generate both the code and the proof that it meets the spec, and the machine checks that part completely. What's left for humans is validating the specification, which is usually much shorter and much more declarative. It says what should happen, not how. That's a far more tractable thing to review.

It also changes how you think about scaling. As these systems get more capable, they'll produce far more code than anyone can read. Verification scales with compute. Human review doesn't. So you want to push as much of the trust as possible onto the verifiable side and keep the validation step as small and clear as you can. And over time, I think AI can help with validation too: suggesting test cases, explaining what a spec implies, finding edge cases where the spec might not match intent. But the final judgment there stays with people, and keeping that boundary explicit is what makes the whole thing trustworthy.

r001.rationale: It says verification checks whether code satisfies a formal specification and that a proof checker checks the proof.

r002.rationale: It defines validation as judging whether the specification captures what people intended.

r003.rationale: It says the connection between a formal specification and human intent cannot be fully formalized and requires human judgment.

r004.rationale: It does not state that a property can be easy to specify yet difficult to prove for a program.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the distinction matters because the two words answer fundamentally different questions, and conflating them is where a lot of the confusion around AI-generated code comes from.

Verification asks: does this program actually do what the specification says? That's a mathematical question. If you have a formal spec and a proof that the implementation satisfies it, you've closed that question completely, and you can check it mechanically. Validation asks something much messier: is the specification itself the right one? Does it capture what the human actually wanted? That's not a mathematical question at all. It's a question about intent, about the world, about what people meant when they wrote a sentence in English.

With AI systems generating code, this separation becomes really important, because the failure modes are so different. If a model writes a program and we can formally verify it against a spec, then the entire remaining risk has been pushed into the spec. The model can't sneak a bug past a proof checker. What it can do is satisfy a spec that was subtly wrong, or incomplete, or that didn't say anything about some property we cared about but forgot to write down. So verification essentially concentrates all of the hard problem into one place, which is a huge win, because now you know exactly where to look.

And I'd argue the specification is usually much smaller and much more readable than the implementation. A sorting spec is two lines. The optimized sorting algorithm might be hundreds of lines of very clever code. So if a human has to review something, they should be reviewing the two lines, not the hundreds. The machine handles the correspondence between them. That's the right division of labor between people and systems: humans do validation, where judgment about intent is required, and machines do verification, where they're far more reliable than we are.

The danger of blurring the two is that people start trusting the wrong thing. They see the word "verified" and assume it means "correct in every sense that matters," when really it means "correct relative to this particular statement." Or, going the other direction, they see that formal methods can't capture intent and dismiss them as useless, when in fact they remove an enormous class of errors. Keeping the concepts separate lets you be honest about what guarantees you actually have, and I think that honesty is going to be essential as more and more code is written by systems we don't fully understand.

r001.rationale: The response says that a proof can establish that an implementation satisfies a formal specification and that this can be checked mechanically.

r002.rationale: It defines validation as checking whether the specification captures what the human intended, a matter of intent and judgment.

r003.rationale: It says that deciding whether the specification captures human intent is not a mathematical question and requires judgment about what people meant, conveying why that alignment cannot itself be formally verified.

r004.rationale: The response says a sorting specification can be short while its implementation is complex, but does not state that an easy-to-specify property can be difficult to prove for a program.

astra-6.text:
Because they answer two different questions. Formal verification asks, “Does this program satisfy the specification?” Validation asks, “Does the specification actually capture what we wanted?” You can have a perfectly verified program that solves the wrong problem because the specification is incomplete or incorrect.

With AI-generated programs, that distinction is particularly useful. The AI can propose code and a proof, and a proof checker can establish that the code meets the formal requirements. But that doesn’t establish that those requirements reflect the user’s intent. You still need validation through examples, testing, and discussion with the people who understand the task.

So the benefit is that we isolate the uncertainty. We can get a very strong guarantee about the relationship between the code and its specification, while being explicit that choosing the right specification remains a separate responsibility.

r001.rationale: It says formal verification checks whether the program satisfies its specification and that a proof checker can establish the code meets the formal requirements.

r002.rationale: It defines validation as checking whether the specification captures what people wanted or the user's intent.

r003.rationale: It separates choosing the right specification from verification, but does not say that alignment cannot be formally verified because interpreting intent involves subjective judgment.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a property being easy to specify but difficult to prove.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is important because these are two different questions. Formal verification asks, “Does this program satisfy the specification?” Validation asks, “Is this specification actually what we wanted?” You can prove a program correct with respect to a specification and still have a program that solves the wrong problem, because the specification leaves something out or encodes the wrong assumption.

With AI-generated programs, formal verification gives us a way to check the output without having to trust the model that produced it. The model can propose a solution, and a proof checker can check that it satisfies the stated requirements. But that doesn’t remove the need to validate those requirements against the intended use. Separating the two makes clear what the proof guarantees and where human judgment and empirical testing are still needed.

r001.rationale: It says formal verification asks whether the program satisfies its specification and describes a proof checker checking that the program meets the stated requirements.

r002.rationale: It describes validation as checking whether the specification is what was wanted and whether the requirements match the intended use.

r003.rationale: It mentions that human judgment is still needed, but does not state that matching a formal specification to an informal one cannot itself be formally verified because interpreting the informal specification is subjective.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss properties that are easy to specify but difficult to prove for a program.
